Behind the image

What is calculated, and what is drawn.

Every ray is traced exactly through the glass in two dimensions. At each surface, flat or curved, the new direction comes from Snell’s law in vector form, with the exact surface normal; when no refracted ray exists, the light is totally reflected. Curved surfaces are true circular arcs, not polygons.

n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂

Speed

Light travels at c / n in glass. The pulses move along each ray at that speed, so they bunch up inside glass, and the lines joining pulses that left together are the wavefronts. Each ray takes the path of least time between its ends (Fermat’s principle).

Partial reflection

At each surface some light is reflected, as given by the Fresnel equations for unpolarised light: about 4% for glass of n = 1.5 at normal incidence, rising towards 100% at grazing angles. Reflected rays are drawn fainter in proportion, and followed while they keep at least 3% of the light.

Glass and colour

The slider sets the index n at 587.6 nm (yellow). Other colours use a Cauchy formula fitted to crown glass (Abbe number about 64), so violet is bent more than red. The prism is dense flint glass, with 2.6 times the dispersion (Abbe number about 25), as in most demonstration prisms. Ray colours are the colours of those wavelengths (approximately, on a screen).

Lens and image

The lens is a thick biconvex lens with spherical surfaces. Its focal length is checked against the lensmaker’s equation. The image is placed where the traced rays nearest the axis cross; rays through the edge of the lens cross noticeably short (spherical aberration, strong for so curved a lens). The lens formula 1/u + 1/v = 1/f is applied with u and v measured from the lens’s principal planes, as it must be for a thick lens.

Touch and keys

Drag to orbit, pinch or scroll to zoom. Keys: Space pause, 1–5 experiments, T Bench/Top.

Drawn for clarity: the thickness of the glass blocks, the printed look of rays and pulses, the pulse spacing and the speed of the animation (real light would cross the bench in about a nanosecond). The optics are two-dimensional (a slice through the middle of each element), so they show exactly how rays bend but not effects of the third dimension. Diffraction and interference, the wave side of light, are on the Light as a wave page.
